injuryResponse.title: Injured Animal Field Response
injuryResponse.subtitle: How to triage, stabilise and move an injured animal without making the injury worse.

sections.title: Make the Scene Safe
sections.text: A second casualty helps nobody. Traffic, fire and water are dealt with before the animal.
bullets: Stop somewhere safe, hazard lights on, and cone or flag the area if you can.
Approach slowly, from the side, speaking softly and avoiding sudden movement.
Protect your arms with a towel, jacket or blanket before touching it.

sections.title: Triage in Sixty Seconds
sections.text: Stand back and read the whole animal: breathing effort, gum colour, bleeding, and whether all four legs move. The loudest problem is rarely the most urgent one.

sections.title: Stop Bleeding First
sections.text: Severe bleeding kills long before a broken bone matters. Firm direct pressure is almost always enough.
bullets: Press a clean pad firmly onto the wound and hold it for three minutes.
Never remove a soaked pad — stack another one on top of it.
Reserve a tourniquet for a limb you genuinely cannot stop any other way.

sections.title: Protect Suspected Fractures
sections.text: Assume a spinal injury in any animal hit by a vehicle. Movement can turn a survivable injury into permanent paralysis.
bullets: Do not straighten a limb and do not bandage a suspected spine.
Slide the animal onto a board, cardboard sheet or folded blanket to move it.
Keep movement to the absolute minimum and pad around the body so it cannot roll.

sections.title: Transport to the Right Place
sections.text: Phone ahead so a team is waiting — arriving unannounced often means being triaged behind scheduled surgery.
bullets: Cover the carrier; darkness and quiet measurably reduce panic.
Keep the vehicle warm and limit handling to essential checks.
Carry the animal straight indoors; never leave it in a parked car.

sections.title: Hand Over the Full Picture
sections.text: What you saw at the scene is diagnostic information the clinic cannot recreate. Give it before you leave, in writing if you can.

checklist.title: What to tell the clinic
items: Species, approximate age and estimated weight.
Where it was found and what most likely caused the injury.
When it happened and how it behaved at the scene.
Every injury you can see, including bleeding from nose, mouth or ears.
Any treatment you gave — pressure, bandaging, water or medication.
Time of last food, water and urination.

items.label: Emergency clinic
items.value: Phone ahead and describe the injuries

injuryResponse.disclaimer: Field care stabilises; it does not treat. Any animal with breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding or a suspected spinal injury needs a veterinarian immediately.
